tx.t: In today's lecture we will study volcanoes and the damage they can do. There are around one thousand three hundred and fifty potentially active volcanoes in the world.
About three quarters of them lie around the Pacific Ocean, in an area called the Ring of Fire. In the year seventy-nine, the eruption of Mount Vesuvius buried the Roman town of Pompeii.

In eighteen fifteen, Mount Tambora in Indonesia erupted so violently that the following year became known as the year without a summer. Scientists measure small earthquakes and gas emissions to try to predict eruptions.

tx.t: Today I want to explain why sleep is so important, and what happens in the brain during the night. Adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep a night, while teenagers need eight to ten.

A full cycle of sleep lasts about ninety minutes, and we go through four or five cycles each night. Most vivid dreams happen during a stage called REM sleep, when the eyes move quickly under the eyelids.

While we sleep, the brain moves memories from short-term storage into long-term storage. Lack of sleep makes it harder to concentrate and slows reaction times, which is why tired drivers cause many accidents.
On average, people spend about one third of their lives asleep.

tx.t: This lecture looks at the history and the future of electric cars. Electric vehicles are older than many people think. The first ones appeared in the eighteen thirties.
Around the year nineteen hundred, more than a quarter of the cars on American roads were electric. Petrol cars then became cheaper and could travel further, so electric cars almost disappeared.

Modern electric cars use lithium-ion batteries, which store more energy for their weight. Their main advantage is that they produce no exhaust gases while driving, though making the batteries does cause pollution.

tx.t: Today I would like to talk about the Great Barrier Reef, the largest coral reef system in the world. It lies off the coast of Queensland in north-eastern Australia.
It stretches for roughly two thousand three hundred kilometres. It is not one reef but a network of nearly three thousand individual reefs.
More than one thousand five hundred species of fish live there, together with many kinds of turtles and sharks. It was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in nineteen eighty-one.
Warm water causes corals to expel the algae that feed them, which turns them white. This is called bleaching.

tx.t: Today I would like to outline what glaciers are, and why they matter for sea level. Glaciers cover about ten per cent of the world's land area.
Together, glaciers and ice sheets store about two thirds of the world's fresh water. A glacier forms when snow builds up for many years and is pressed into dense ice.
Since nineteen hundred, the global sea level has risen by about twenty centimetres. This rise is caused partly by melting ice and partly because warm water takes up more space.

tx.t: Today I would like to describe a bike-sharing scheme in the town of Stanbridge. It began in twenty ten with five hundred and thirty-four bikes, placed at stations around the centre.
Use grew quickly. Within three years the number of journeys had risen by sixty-six per cent, and on a busy day there were more than twelve thousand trips.
The scheme soon met a serious problem: empty stations at rush hour. The council solved it with a mobile app that shows where bikes are available.
Today, a ride costs two pounds twenty-five for the first half hour, and the first fifteen minutes are free for residents.
